content.subtitle: Resources are limited, so every choice has a cost.
content.outcome: Explain scarcity and identify tradeoffs created by limited resources
content.core: Scarcity means people, businesses, and governments have limited resources but unlimited wants. Because resources such as time, money, labor, and raw materials are limited, choices must be made. Every choice involves a tradeoff, and those tradeoffs force individuals and societies to decide how to use scarce resources. Scarcity is the basic problem that economics studies.
recognition: Resources are limited, but wants are greater than what can be produced.
A choice must be made between competing uses.
Getting more of one thing means giving up something else.
The question focuses on limits, tradeoffs, or unmet wants.
content.watch: Scarcity does not mean there is almost none of a good. It means the good is limited relative to wants. Even time and money are scarce because they have alternative uses.
content.worked: A student has two hours before an exam and must choose between studying economics or finishing a history paper. The student cannot fully do both. This is scarcity because time is limited, so choosing one use means giving up the other.
content.check: A city has enough money to build either a new park or repair several roads, but not both this year. Why is this an example of scarcity?

Scarcity forces a choice; the best forgone use created by that choice is its opportunity cost. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative, not every alternative added together. The next best option is the $80 shift. A valuable nonmonetary alternative can be the next-best option forgone.

content.subtitle: Competition limits how much control one buyer or seller has over price.
content.outcome: Identify the conditions that create price-taking behavior and limited market power
content.core: A competitive market contains many independent buyers and sellers, usually trading products that buyers view as close substitutes. No single participant controls enough of the market to set the market price. A small firm is therefore a price taker: it chooses how much to sell at the price created by market supply and demand. Competition becomes stronger when firms can enter or exit, buyers can compare offers, and switching among sellers is easy.
recognition: Many independent firms sell the same product or close substitutes.
One seller supplies only a small share of total market output.
A firm accepts a price determined by overall market supply and demand.
Buyers can compare prices and switch sellers without much difficulty.
Entry by new firms or exit by existing firms changes competitive pressure.
content.watch: A market is not strictly competitive just because it has several sellers. Product differentiation, search costs, network effects, or barriers to entry can still give firms pricing power. The key question is whether one seller can raise its price persistently without losing many customers to available alternatives.
content.worked: A wheat farmer is one of thousands selling a standardized crop. The posted market price is $6 per bushel. If this farmer asks $7 while other farmers still charge $6, buyers can purchase identical wheat elsewhere. The farmer is too small to move the market price, so raising the price would sharply reduce sales. The evidence - many sellers, a standardized product, and easy switching - identifies price-taking behavior.
